chapter: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
title: Trying bebop on audiences; analyzing 'Night in Tunisia'; Hawkins plays bop
summary: Dancers walked off when he played bop; he learned the notes by testing chords against 'A Night in Tunisia'. Hawkins eventually played it well, but Horace insists you must know your instrument.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: And if I -- I had a few bebop numbers in my group, but I tested this out, and I played places. We played bebop, and some of the people looked at us like we were crazy. They'd walk off the floor. After, I previously played just a little old, hard kind of standard tune, and they liked it. Soon as I go into this bebop, or a guy would play something, the people would look at -- look strange, you know? So I said, they don't dig this. But musically, all right. I had things like da-doo-doo-dee-doo-doo-dee-doo-doo-duh -- bee-ee, ba-ba-bop, all that stuff. That's strictly bebop, (inaudible) the bebop, you know. And I've got it in my books now. We played sometimes when maybe somebody will ask for something like that, you know. I can't even think of the name of that tune right now, I can play them in there.
I know it well, and I can't think of it either.
I tell you what I used to do, though.

" Night in Tunisia. " I used to take that thing and all the other bebop things and hit a chord and used to diagnose and sample the notes that were in the bebop thing they played, and, man, they were there.

They laid, (Inaudible), they were right in there. And I said, this is it. And this is one of the ways that I got to play a little bit like it, because I know what it consisted of, you know, but I was amazed at the way that the jumping with this, you know, with the notes there were.

Yeah, the leaps. But these guys -- that made me respect Dizzy more, one of those things. But I just figured that that I couldn't make a career of it, you know, and guys, as you said, Louie didn't accept it, a lot of guys. Hawk didn't accept it for a long time, but you knew him --
He was one guy that really --
Man, later on Hawk made some records, and I said, " listen to Hawk playing this bop. "
And, man, he could play it.
He gathered some of the beboppers around him --
-- and he did play it, yeah.

Because when it first came out, I remember Hawk's reaction about this thing, and he said, 'Well, this is what I'm going to have to get with, you know, and he did, and, man, he could play it. But I still contend that you've got to know your instrument, and you've got to know the chord, something about it. You just don't play this by ear. Now you never did catch Red Allen, guys like that playing bebop. See? Gail Brockman was another guy, trumpet player, that, he played a little, but the fundamentals, man, you had to know what you were doing, you had to know your horn, see.

And so I just decided to pass it up and not go that route. But I enjoy listening to it; even today I do, especially when the guys play it and it makes sense. I don't mean these little, young -- because I had this little trumpet player, Benny Harris, and he made some one nighters with me, and he played that stuff, man. And he would come behind that bebop and start swinging. And then he'd go back into the bebop, and he was versatile (inaudible), you know. That little cat could play, man! So I have nothing against it. I just didn't accept it as a career.
